title: Turbulence is a cascade of eddies, and averaging it leaves a stress you have to model
summary: Energy enters a turbulent flow at large scales and is passed down to small ones, which is why the spectrum falls as k to the minus five thirds. Averaging the equations hides the eddies but leaves the Reynolds stress, and every closure is a way of guessing it.

media.alt: Log-log plot of an energy spectrum E(k) for wavenumber k from 1 to about 300. A teal curve falls in a nearly straight line through the middle range, a dashed orange reference line of slope minus five thirds runs parallel just above it, and at the highest wavenumbers the curve bends steeply downward.
media.caption: Reference render of plot class F10.3 with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery), not a project result.

source.note: Standard turbulence theory (Reynolds 1895 averaging, Kolmogorov 1941 scaling, eddy-viscosity and anisotropy ideas as in textbooks). The figure is the design system's synthetic F10.3 render, so no project number is quoted.

read_the_figure.question: Is there a range of scales where energy is passed down without being created or destroyed, and does its slope match the theory?
read_the_figure.axes: x: wavenumber $k$ (inverse length) on a log scale, so large eddies are on the left and small ones on the right. y: energy per unit wavenumber $E(k)$ on a log scale.
look_at: The dashed line has slope $-5/3$. It is a reference, not data: the question is whether the solid curve runs parallel to it over a decade or more.
Left of the straight part is the energy-containing range, where the flow geometry sets the shape. Right of it the curve drops steeply: viscosity removes energy at the smallest eddies.
A straight stretch on log-log axes is a power law, so equal steps in $k$ always change $E$ by the same factor.
The width of the straight part grows with Reynolds number: a low-Reynolds flow may have none.
read_the_figure.proves: A decade of slope $-5/3$ is evidence of an inertial range, where energy is handed from scale to scale at the rate $\varepsilon$ with no direct effect of viscosity or forcing.
if_wrong: No straight stretch: the Reynolds number is too low, or the grid or filter has removed the scales that should show it.
A bend or pile-up at the highest $k$: aliasing, numerical dissipation or a filter, not physics.
A slope that depends on how many points you fit: report the fitting range, because a short window can be bent to match any exponent.
must_check: Both axes logarithmic, with a slope triangle or reference line of exactly $-5/3$.
The fitted range of $k$ marked, and the Kolmogorov scale $k_\eta=1/\eta$ shown if known.
Spectrum units stated, and whether it is 1D or 3D (their prefactors differ).
Whether the data are measured, simulated or synthetic.

terms.meaning: Writing each flow quantity as a mean plus a fluctuation, so that the mean of the fluctuation is zero.
The average momentum carried by the fluctuations, $\overline{u_i'u_j'}$ times density. It acts on the mean flow like an extra stress.
Half the trace of the Reynolds stress per unit mass: the energy in the fluctuations.
The rate at which viscosity turns turbulent kinetic energy into heat, per unit mass. In steady turbulence it equals the rate energy is fed in.
The transfer of energy from large eddies to smaller ones until the eddies are small enough for viscosity to act.
How the kinetic energy is distributed over wavenumber, so that its integral is the kinetic energy.
The size at which viscosity ends the cascade, built from $\nu$ and $\varepsilon$ alone.
The symmetric and antisymmetric parts of the velocity gradient: stretching and shearing versus spinning.
Q is half of the rotation squared minus the strain squared. Regions with $Q>0$ are where spin beats strain: vortex cores.
A modelling coefficient that makes the Reynolds stress act like a viscous stress, proportional to the mean strain.
How far the Reynolds stress is from equal in all directions. It is zero for isotropic turbulence.

remember: The averaged momentum equation has the extra term $-\partial_j(\rho\,\overline{u_i'u_j'})$: more unknowns than equations, so a closure is needed.
Boussinesq: $-\overline{u_i'u_j'}+\tfrac23k\delta_{ij}=2\nu_tS_{ij}$. It forces the normal stresses to be equal in a simple shear, which real shear flows do not satisfy.

understand.title: Intuition
understand.text: Stir a cup and the flow breaks into eddies; the big ones break into smaller ones, and so on until the eddies are so small that viscosity smears them out. Energy only goes down the cascade, one scale at a time, and at the bottom it becomes heat. The spectrum is a ledger of how much energy sits at each size. Averaging smooths all this away, but the average flow still feels the momentum the eddies carry, and that is the Reynolds stress.

understand.title: Why the exponent is not a fitted number
understand.text: In the middle of the cascade the only quantity a scale can know about is the rate $\varepsilon$ at which energy is passing through it, plus its own size. Viscosity has not acted yet and the forcing is far away. Two quantities with fixed units leave exactly one way to build an energy spectrum, and that fixes the exponent. This is a dimensional argument, not a derivation from the equations, and it is checked by experiment.

understand.title: The hard tier
understand.text: The $-5/3$ law is for the average spectrum of homogeneous, isotropic turbulence at high Reynolds number. Real flows show small deviations (intermittency) and are not isotropic near walls, in shear layers or around vortices. The eddy-viscosity model replaces a tensor with a scalar times the strain, and fails exactly where anisotropy and history matter: strongly swirling flow, separation, and flows with sudden strain. Models that carry the stress components themselves, or add corrections, exist for that reason.

steps.title: Reynolds decomposition and the mean of a product
steps.note: The cross terms $U v'$ and $V u'$ average to zero. Checked numerically on a correlated sample, where the identity holds to machine precision.

steps.title: Averaging the momentum equation
steps.note: Incompressibility lets the nonlinear term be written $\partial_j(u_iu_j)$. Its average is $\partial_j(U_iU_j+\overline{u_i'u_j'})$, and the second part moves to the right as a stress.

steps.title: The closure problem by counting
steps.note: The Reynolds stress is symmetric, so it adds six unknowns. Writing a transport equation for it adds triple correlations, and so on without end: every level of averaging creates a new unknown.

steps.title: Constant flux through the cascade
steps.note: A scale $\ell=1/k$ with velocity $u_k$ turns over in time $1/(k u_k)$ and so passes energy $u_k^2$ per turnover at rate $k u_k^3$. In the inertial range this rate is the same at every $k$ and equals $\varepsilon$, so $u_k\sim(\varepsilon/k)^{1/3}$.

steps.title: Kolmogorov's spectrum by dimensional analysis
steps.note: Solved symbolically: $a=2/3$, $b=-5/3$. It agrees with the previous step, since $E\,k\sim u_k^2\sim\varepsilon^{2/3}k^{-2/3}$. The constant $C$ is of order one and is measured, not derived.

steps.title: Where the cascade ends
steps.note: With only $\nu$ and $\varepsilon$, the only length is $\eta$ (checked by solving for the exponents). Setting $\varepsilon\sim u'^3/\ell$ gives the second relation: the range of scales widens with $Re$.

steps.title: Strain and rotation: split the velocity gradient
steps.note: $S$ stretches and shears fluid elements, $\Omega$ spins them without deforming them. Simple shear has both in equal measure; solid rotation has only $\Omega$.

steps.title: The Q-criterion
steps.note: The middle equality is verified symbolically for a general $3\times3$ gradient. The last follows from the divergence of the momentum equation for incompressible flow: where $Q>0$ the pressure has a minimum, which is why vortex cores are low-pressure tubes.

steps.title: Q in three canonical flows
steps.note: All three computed symbolically from the velocity fields. A Rankine vortex is solid rotation in its core ($Q>0$) and a free vortex outside ($Q<0$), so the iso-surface $Q>0$ picks out the core and stops at its edge.

steps.title: Eddy viscosity and why it needs the anisotropy
steps.note: The trace of both sides is zero, so the model is consistent, and $k^2/\varepsilon$ has units of $\mathrm{m^2/s}$ as a viscosity must ($C_\mu\approx0.09$ in the common $k$-$\varepsilon$ model). In a simple shear $S_{11}=S_{22}=S_{33}=0$, so the model predicts $b_{11}=b_{22}=b_{33}=0$: no normal-stress differences at all.

worked.title: How small are the smallest eddies, and what would a direct simulation cost?
worked.problem: Air ($\nu=1.5\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}$) is stirred with fluctuations $u'=1\ \mathrm{m/s}$ at the large scale $\ell=0.1\ \mathrm{m}$. Find $Re$, the dissipation rate, the Kolmogorov scale and the number of grid points a direct simulation of one box of side $\ell$ needs.

solution.text: Ratio of scales, and the matching power of $Re$.
Grid points in 3D if the cell is about $\eta$.

worked.answer: The smallest eddies are about 0.14 mm across, 738 times smaller than the stirring scale, and resolving all of them in a box of side 0.1 m takes of the order of $4\times10^{8}$ cells. This is why most engineering flows are averaged and closed with a model. Numbers computed and checked with a script; $\varepsilon\sim u'^3/\ell$ is an order-of-magnitude estimate.

analyze.q: Show that in a simple shear flow the eddy-viscosity model gives equal normal stresses, and say what measurements of near-wall turbulence show instead.
analyze.hint: Compute $S_{11}$, $S_{22}$, $S_{33}$ for $U=\gamma y$ and use the model; compare with $\overline{u'^2}>\overline{v'^2}$ in boundary layers.

analyze.q: A computed spectrum is straight with slope $-5/3$ between $k=5$ and $k=15$ only. Is that an inertial range?
analyze.hint: How many factors of the base is that, and what would you want on both sides?

analyze.q: A Q iso-surface at a value close to zero fills the whole domain, while a larger value shows thin tubes. What does the threshold decide?
analyze.hint: Think of the sign of $Q$ in a shear layer far from any core.

evaluate.q: A paper chooses its closure because its $k$-$\varepsilon$ run matches the mean velocity profile. What other evidence would you ask for before trusting it on a swirling flow?
evaluate.hint: The mean can be right while the stresses are wrong.

evaluate.q: Two groups report the exponent $-1.5$ and $-1.7$ from the same spectrum. How can both be right, and how would you settle it?
evaluate.hint: Fit range, noise at the high-$k$ end, and a compensated plot $k^{5/3}E$.

create: Design a figure that shows a Lumley-triangle trajectory across a boundary layer from the wall to the free stream. What would you plot, and which corners would you label?
Choose a compensated spectrum $k^{5/3}E(k)/\varepsilon^{2/3}$ plot for a dataset. What does a flat plateau tell you, and what height should it have?

checks.q: Why can't the averaged equations be solved without a model?
checks.hint: Count unknowns and equations after averaging.
checks.answer: Averaging the nonlinear term leaves $\overline{u_i'u_j'}$, six new unknowns, while the number of equations stays four. Its own transport equation contains triple correlations, so every new equation brings a new unknown. A model (closure) must relate the stress to the mean flow.

checks.q: By dimensional analysis, what exponent of $k$ does an energy spectrum that depends only on $\varepsilon$ and $k$ have?
checks.hint: Match powers of metres and seconds.

checks.q: For solid rotation at angular speed $\omega=2\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and for a simple shear $U=\gamma y$ with $\gamma=2\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, what is $Q$ in each, and what does that say?
checks.hint: Solid rotation has $S=0$; shear has equal $S$ and $\Omega$.
checks.answer: $Q=\omega^2=4\ \mathrm{s^{-2}}$ for the rotation and $Q=0$ for the shear. Both have the same vorticity magnitude, but only the first is a vortex: $Q$ asks whether rotation beats strain, not just whether the fluid spins.

checks.q: A $k$-$\varepsilon$ simulation of a fully developed pipe flow gets the mean profile right. Is that enough to conclude the model captures the turbulence?
checks.hint: What does the model assume about normal stresses?
checks.answer: No. A good mean profile only shows that the shear stress is about right. The model predicts equal normal stresses by construction, so the anisotropy, and anything that depends on it (secondary flows in ducts, for example), is not tested. Compare stresses, not just the mean.

checks.q: You have a time series of velocity at a point in a turbulent flow. How would you make a spectrum and decide whether it has an inertial range?
checks.hint: FFT, averaging and a compensated plot.
checks.answer: Split the record into overlapping windows, apply a window function, take the FFT and average the power spectra. Plot on log-log axes with a $k^{-5/3}$ reference and also $k^{5/3}E$. A flat plateau over a decade or more, well away from the energy-containing scales and the noise floor, is an inertial range. Convert frequency to wavenumber with Taylor's frozen-turbulence assumption only if the fluctuations are small compared with the mean speed.
